body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of History of Formula One

Formula One automobile racing has its roots in the European Grand Prix championships of the 1920s and 1930s. The modern era officially began in 1946 when the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) standardised a set of engine and chassis rules, which led to the inaugural FIA World Championship of Drivers in 1950 at the Silverstone Circuit.

The history of Formula One is marked by the evolution of its technical regulations, and distinct periods of team and driver dominance. Significant mechanical developments include the mid-engine layout shift in the late 1950s, ground-effect aerodynamics and turbocharging in the 1970s and 1980s, active suspension in the 1990s, and 1.6-liter V6 turbo-hybrid power units introduced in 2014. These technical shifts coincided with dominant eras for constructors including Alfa Romeo, Ferrari, Cooper, Lotus, Williams, McLaren, Mercedes and Red Bull.

Driver safety regulation transformed significantly following driver casualties in the 1960s, 1970s and 1994, leading to mandatory circuit updates, structural crash standards, and cockpit protection systems such as the halo.
